title: Ghadar, 1913
hookLine: Sikh workers in North America founded a party to free India

lines: A SAWMILL ON THE PACIFIC COAST.
cards: A sawmill on the Pacific coast. The shift is over, the saws go quiet, and a group of men in turbans sit down together on wooden crates. They cut timber and work farm rows for low pay, a long way from their villages.
Someone has a newspaper printed in Gurmukhi and Urdu, and reads it aloud, because not everyone can read. The talk isn't about wages.
It's about home: a land under a foreign government, and whether men this far away can still do something for it.

teach.b: Punjabi migrants, many of them Sikh, had gone to Canada and the United States to work in mills, on railways and on farms.
Abroad they met hard treatment, and some began to ask why their own country wasn't free to protect them.
In 1913 they founded an organization on the American West Coast to work for India's freedom from British rule. Sohan Singh Bhakna is remembered as one of its leaders, alongside the scholar Har Dayal.
Its newspaper was called Ghadar, a word usually given as revolt or uprising, and soon the movement took the same name. It wasn't a Sikh religious body.
Its members were Sikh, Hindu and Muslim, and its papers spoke of India as a whole. But Sikh workers filled its ranks, and gurdwaras abroad were where its members met.

Tradition says Guru Arjan wrote the verses at Ang 96 of the Guru Granth Sahib while he was sent away from his father, the Guru. He sings of a mind that longs to see the Guru, the way a thirsty bird longs for rain.
Those lines are about longing for the Guru, not for a country. But they say something plainly: distance doesn't cancel love. It can sharpen it.
An ocean away from Punjab, the Ghadar workers' care for it didn't fade.

how: Sikhs in North America and in Punjab remember the Ghadar movement as part of their community's history abroad, and its story is told in gurdwaras, museums and community events, especially among the diaspora on the Pacific coast.

practice: Bring to mind one person who lives a long way from where they grew up: a grandparent who emigrated, a friend working abroad, a neighbor who sends money back home.
Picture them at the end of a long day, thinking of a place they can't easily reach, and breathe slowly with them in mind. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, holding that person close.
